exercise_group.instruction: Compute the determinants in Exercises 1–8 using a cofactor expansion across the first row. In Exercises 1–4, also compute the determinant by a cofactor expansion down the second column.
Compute the determinants in Exercises 9–14 by cofactor expansions. At each step, choose a row or column that involves the least amount of computation.

exercise_group.instruction: The expansion of a $$3 \times 3$$ determinant can be remembered by the following device. Write a second copy of the first two columns to the right of the matrix, and compute the determinant by multiplying entries on six diagonals:

Add the downward diagonal products and subtract the upward products. Use this method to compute the determinants in Exercises 15–18. Warning: This trick does not generalize in any reasonable way to $$4 \times 4$$ or larger matrices.
In Exercises 19–24, explore the effect of an elementary row operation on the determinant of a matrix. In each case, state the row operation and describe how it affects the determinant.

Use Exercises 25–30 to answer the questions in Exercises 31 and 32. Give reasons for your answers.

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 33–36, verify that $$\det EA = \text{(det} E \text{)(det} A)$$ , where $$E$$ is the elementary matrix shown and $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and let $$k$$ be a scalar. Find a formula that relates $$\det kA$$ to $$k$$ and $$\det A$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 39 through 42, $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) An $$n \times n$$ determinant is defined by determinants of $$(n - 1) \times (n - 1)$$ submatrices.
(T/F) The $$\left(\right. i , j \left.\right)$$ $$\text{-cofactor}$$ of a matrix $$A$$ is the matrix $$A_{ij}$$ obtained by deleting from $$A$$ its $$i \text{th}$$ row and $$j \text{th}$$ column.
(T/F) The cofactor expansion of $$\det A$$ down a column is equal to the cofactor expansion along a row.
(T/F) The determinant of a triangular matrix is the sum of the entries on the main diagonal.

Let $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Compute the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\textbf{u}$$ , $$\textbf{v}$$ , $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ , and $$\textbf{0}$$ , and compute the determinant of $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \textbf{u} & \textbf{v} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . How do they compare? Replace the first entry of $$\textbf{v}$$ by an arbitrary number $$x$$ , and repeat the problem. Draw a picture and explain what you find.

Let $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} c \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , where $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ are positive (for simplicity). Compute the area of the parallelogram determined by $$\textbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ , and $$\textbf{0}$$ , and compute the determinants of the matrices $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \textbf{u} & \textbf{v} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} \textbf{v} & \textbf{u} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Draw a picture and explain what you find.

Let $$A$$ be a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix all of whose entries are numbers that are greater than or equal to $$- 5$$ and less than or equal to $$5$$ . Decide if each of the following is a reasonable answer for $$\det A$$ .

[T] Construct a random $$4 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ with integer entries between $$- 9$$ and $$9$$ . How is $$\det A^{- 1}$$ related to $$\det A$$ ? Experiment with random $$n \times n$$ integer matrices for $$n = 4$$ , $$5$$ , and $$6$$ , and make a conjecture. Note: In the unlikely event that you encounter a matrix with a zero determinant, reduce it to echelon form and discuss what you find.

[T] Is it true that $$\text{det} AB = \text{(det} A \text{)(det} B)$$ ? To find out, generate random $$5 \times 5$$ matrices $$A$$ and $$B$$ , and compute $$\text{det} AB - \text{(det} A \text{det} B)$$ . Repeat the calculations for three other pairs of $$n \times n$$ matrices, for various values of $$n$$ . Report your results.
[T] Is it true that $$\text{det(} A + B) = \text{det} A + \text{det} B$$ ? Experiment with four pairs of random matrices as in Exercise 48, and make a conjecture.

[T] Construct a random $$4 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ with integer entries between $$- 9$$ and $$9$$ , and compare $$\det A$$ with $$\det A^{T}$$ , $$\det ( - A)$$ , $$\det (2A)$$ , and $$\det (10A)$$ . Repeat with two other random $$4 \times 4$$ integer matrices, and make conjectures about how these determinants are related. (Refer to Exercise 44 in Section 2.1.) Then check your conjectures with several random $$5 \times 5$$ and $$6 \times 6$$ integer matrices. Modify your conjectures, if necessary, and report your results.

[T] Recall from the introductory section that the larger the determinant of $$D^{T}D$$ , where $$D$$ is the design matrix, the better will be the accuracy of the calculated weights for small light objects. Which of the following matrices corresponds to the best design for four weighings of four objects? Describe which of the objects $$s_{1}$$ , $$s_{2}$$ , $$s_{3}$$ , and $$s_{4}$$ you would put in the left and right pans for each weighing corresponding to the best design matrix.
